السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي - سودان تربيون
sudan.content: السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English السبت , 24 أكتوبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية اختيار المحرر السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي اختيار المحرر السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي 24 أكتوبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , الأخبار 0 أفراد من بعثة يونيسفا يخمدون الحريق الذي اندلع في سوق النعام، عقب الهجوم الذي أسفر عن مقتل 80 شخصًا. الخرطوم 24 أكتوبر 2026 – دعا رئيس اللجنة الإشرافية لمنطقة أبيي من جانب السودان الخير أبو مريدات، السبت، بعثة الأمم المتحدة الأمنية المؤقتة “يونيسفا” إلى إجراء تحقيق وتحديد الجهات المسؤولة عن الهجوم على سوق النعام. ونفذت طائرات مسيّرة في 19 أكتوبر الحالي، هجوماً على سوق النعام، المعروف أيضاً باسم ” أميت”، أسفر عن مقتل 80 شخصاً وإصابة 19 آخرين، فيما لا يزال أشخاص في عداد المفقودين، وفقاً للأمم المتحدة. وقال أبو مريدات، في تصريح صحفي، إنه “يدعو بعثة يونيسفا إلى إجراء تحقيق عاجل وشفاف لكشف ملابسات الهجوم على سوق النعام وتحديد الجهات المسؤولة عنه، بما يضمن المساءلة وعدم إفلات المتورطين من العقاب”. وأبدى أسفه إزاء الهجوم وسقوط ضحايا مدنيين، مشدداً على أن حماية أرواح المدنيين وصون أمنهم وسلامتهم تمثل أولوية ومسؤولية أساسية. وأشار إلى أن السودان جاد في الاضطلاع بمسؤولياته تجاه حماية مواطنيه والعمل على تجنيب سكان المنطقة مخاطر الحرب والهجمات المسلحة. والجمعة، نفت وزارة الخارجية السودانية صلة الجيش بالهجوم على سوق النعام، وقالت إنه يشبه القصف الذي شنته قوات الدعم السريع في ديسمبر 2025 على مقر بعثة يونيسفا في كادقلي بجنوب كردفان، والذي أودى بحياة عدد من قوات حفظ السلام. واتهمت وزارة خارجية جنوب السودان الجيش السوداني بتنفيذ الهجوم كما استدعت سفير السودان في جوبا وأبلغته احتجاجها على القصف. وطالب أبو مريدات بضرورة التعامل بحزم مع وجود الجماعات المسلحة الخارجة عن سلطات الدولة والمرتزقة المتنافسين على النفوذ داخل منطقة أبيي أو في محيطها. وأوضح أن التساهل مع هذه المظاهر المسلحة أسهم في تهيئة بيئة أمنية مضطربة تزيد من احتمالات وقوع مثل هذه الحوادث، الأمر الذي يستدعي اتخاذ تدابير جادة وفعالة لمنع تكرارها وحماية المدنيين. وتفرض قوات الدعم السريع ومليشيات متحالفة معها سيطرتها على أجزاء واسعة من سوق النعام، مع فرض ضرائب على حركة التجارة الداخلة إلى دارفور وكردفان. وتحول سوق النعام، بعد اندلاع النزاع في السودان منتصف أبريل 2023، من سوق محلية إلى مركز رئيسي لتجارة الوقود والغذاء ومواد البناء والأدوية، إضافة إلى السلع التي تتدفق من جنوب السودان إلى كردفان ودارفور. وجدد أبو مريدات تأكيد التزام السودان بتعهداته الدولية والاتفاقيات الموقعة بشأن منطقة أبيي، واحترام القرارات الدولية الرامية إلى الحفاظ على أمن المنطقة واستقرارها. وقال إن تحقيق الاستقرار في أبيي يتطلب تعاوناً مسؤولاً والتزاماً عملياً بالاتفاقيات القائمة، والعمل المشترك من أجل حماية المدنيين وصون أمن المنطقة وتجنيب سكانها تداعيات الحرب. وتتنازع الخرطوم وجوبا على السيادة على أبيي الغنية بالنفط، حيث فشل البلدان في الاتفاق على من يحق له المشاركة في استفتاء تقرير مصير المنطقة، المنصوص عليه في اتفاقية السلام الشامل لعام 2005، بسبب رفض قبيلة الدينكا نقوك مشاركة الرحل من قبيلة المسيرية في الاستفتاء. الكلمات: أبيي الامم المتحدة النزاع حول أبيي بعثة يونيسفا سوق النعام مقالات ذات صلة الوساطة: لجنة مصغرة للترتيبات الأمنية بين وفدي الحكومة و(الشعبية) مؤسسة تجمع رجال الأعمال الأميركيين والسودانيين لتنشيط الاستثمار صواريخ تدك مقر الحكومة في شرق دارفور وتواصل الهجمات على نيالا السلطات السودانية تعمم (نشرة حمراء) للقبض على صلاح قوش من اختيار المحرر اختيار المحرر السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي 24 أكتوبر 2026 الحشائش النيلية تهدد محطات المياه في كوستي.. والنيل الأبيض تستنجد بوزارة الري 24 أكتوبر 2026 الأمم المتحدة: مقتل (306) سودانيين بضربات المسيّرات خلال أكتوبر 24 أكتوبر 2026 الأكثر قراءة هذا الأسبوع مطالبات بوضع المواطنين السودانيين في صميم عملية الإصلاح الأمني والعسكري السودان: مجموعة حقوقية تقترح إنشاء مراكز إغاثة وسط تحذيرات دولية من المجاعة الحشائش النيلية تهدد محطات المياه في كوستي.. والنيل الأبيض تستنجد Adel Abdelrheem 24 أكتوبر 2026 • تحديث : 24 أكتوبر 2026 SUDAN الخرطوم/ عادل عبد الرحيم / الأناضول أعلنت لجنة الأمل للعودة الطوعية، السبت، تسيير 25 حافلة تقل 1225 سودانيا من العاصمة المصرية القاهرة إلى السودان، ضمن برنامج العودة الطوعية. وقال رئيس اللجنة محمد وداعة، في تصريحات صحفية بالقاهرة، إن 25 حافلة تحمل على متنها 1225 من طلاب التعليم العام ومنسوبي الخدمة المدنية وأسرهم، بحسب وكالة الأنباء السودانية. ​وأضاف وداعة، أن التفويج شمل اليوم بعض مؤسسات الدولة، ومنسوبي الإذاعة والتلفزيون، والسلطة القضائية، ووزارتي الثروة الحيوانية والعدل، وديوان الحسابات، والطيران المدني. ولفت إلى أن التركيز خلال الفترة الحالية ينصب على إعادة منسوبي الخدمة المدنية، لتمكينهم من استئناف العمل في مؤسساتهم، وفق توجيهات رئيس وزراء البلاد كامل إدريس، مؤخرا. وأكد أن عودة هذه الفئات تمثل خطوة مهمة نحو تحقيق الاستقرار الأسري، بما يسهم بدوره في التنمية المجتمعية. وفي 10 أكتوبر/ تشرين الأول الجاري، أعلنت لجنة الأمل تسيير 18 حافلة تقل 882 سودانيا من القاهرة إلى السودان، ضمن برنامج العودة الطوعية. وخلال سبتمبر/ أيلول الماضي، جرى نقل 4073 سودانيا إلى بلادهم عبر 7 رحلات شملت 83 حافلة، بحسب اللجنة. ومنذ اندلاع الحرب بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع في أبريل/ نيسان 2023، غادر أكثر من 1.2 مليون سوداني إلى مصر، وفق تقديرات رسمية، فيما كان يقيم فيها نحو 5 ملايين سوداني قبل الحرب، لتصبح مصر إحدى أبرز وجهات الفارين من القتال. وحتى نهاية عام 2025، عاد إلى السودان طوعا نحو 428 ألفا و676 شخصا، وفق أرقام سبق أن أعلنها السفير السوداني عبد القادر عبد الله. وجاءت عمليات العودة في أعقاب مبادرة أطلقتها السلطات المصرية في أكتوبر/ تشرين الأول 2025، لنقل السودانيين الراغبين في العودة عبر قطار مخصص من القاهرة إلى أسوان. وأسفرت الحرب، وفق تقديرات أممية ودولية، عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص. وبرنامج العودة الطوعية للسودانيين من مصر هو مبادرة مخصصة لتيسير وتفويج المواطنين السودانيين الراغبين في العودة إلى وطنهم بشكل اختياري ومجاني، وتشرف عليه آلية وطنية تُعرف باسم "لجنة الأمل للعودة الطوعية". news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription السوداني، فيتو - لبنى سعد شارك طباعة 18 حجم الخط سعر الجنيه السوداني ، شهد سعر صرف الدولار الأمريكي استقرارا أمام الجنيه السوداني في البنوك السودانية، مساء اليوم السبت 24 -10-2026. وترصد “فيتو” في السطور التالية آخر حركة لسعر الجنيه السوداني، مقابل الدولار في بنك السودان المركزي . سعر الجنيه السوداني مقابل الدولار في بنك السودان المركزي سعر الشراء: 4200 جنيه سوداني. سعر البيع: 3700 جنيه سوداني. الجنيه السوداني، تاريخ وتحديات العملة الجنيه السوداني هو العملة الرسمية لجمهورية السودان، ويرمز له بالرمز SDG، ويصدره بنك السودان المركزي، ويُستخدم في كافة المعاملات داخل البلاد. وشهد الجنيه السوداني عدة تحولات تاريخية منذ اعتماده، خاصة مع التغيرات الاقتصادية والسياسية التي مرت بها البلاد، بما في ذلك فترات التضخم المرتفع وإعادة هيكلة العملة؛ ما أثر في قيمته أمام العملات الأجنبية، وعلى رأسها الدولار الأمريكي. الفئات الورقية والمعدنية للعملة السودانية الفئات الورقية: -1 جنيه -2 جنيه -5 جنيهات -10 جنيهات -20 جنيهًا -50 جنيهًا -100 جنيه -200 جنيه -500 جنيه العملات المعدنية: -1 جنيه -50 قرشًا -25 قرشًا الجنيه السوداني في الأسواق المحلية والعالمية يواجه الجنيه السوداني تحديات في الأسواق المحلية والعالمية نتيجة عوامل اقتصادية متعددة، منها معدلات التضخم المرتفعة، وتقلبات سعر الصرف ، ونقص العملات الأجنبية. ورغم ذلك، يبذل بنك السودان المركزي جهودًا مستمرة لضبط السوق النقدي من خلال سياسات نقدية تهدف إلى تحقيق الاستقرار النسبي للعملة وتقليل الفجوة بين السعر الرسمي والسوق الموازي. العوامل المؤثرة في سعر الجنيه السوداني • تتأثر حركة الجنيه السوداني أمام الدولار بعدة عوامل رئيسية، أبرزها: • معدلات التضخم المحلية وتأثيرها على القوة الشرائية. • حجم الاحتياطي من النقد الأجنبي لدى بنك السودان المركزي. • تدفقات الصادرات والواردات وحركة التجارة الخارجية. • الاستقرار السياسي والاقتصادي داخل السودان. • نشاط السوق الموازي (السوق السوداء) وتأثيره في السعر الرسمي. نصائح للمستثمرين والمتعاملين • متابعة قرارات بنك السودان المركزي بشكل دوري. • مراقبة تطورات الاقتصاد العالمي وأسعار الدولار. • الحذر من تقلبات السوق الموازي وتأثيرها على الأسعار الرسمية. • تنويع الاستثمارات لتقليل وكردفان وتقدم ميداني للجيش السوداني بمحور النيل الأزرق شهدت العاصمة السويسرية جنيف مشاورات مكثفة بين الولايات المتحدة والمملكة العربية السعودية لبحث خيارات إقرار هدنة إنسانية في السودان. وتهدف هذه التحركات الدبلوماسية إلى التمهيد لوقف دائم لإطلاق النار وإطلاق حوار وطني شامل، مع تنسيق جهود الوساطة الدولية لإنهاء النزاع المستمر. ميدانياً، تصدرت حرب الطائرات المسيرة المشهد القتالي بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع، في ظل تراجع وتيرة المواجهات البرية المباشرة في جبهات دارفور وكردفان. وقد أدى هذا التحول إلى توسيع النطاق الجغرافي للحرب ليشمل مناطق كانت تُصنف سابقاً كأماكن آمنة بعيدة عن الصراع المسلح. أفادت مصادر عسكرية بأن الجيش يشن ضربات جوية متواصلة عبر المسيرات لاستهداف مواقع الدعم السريع وإضعاف قدراتها القتالية. وتسعى هذه العمليات إلى فرض هيمنة جوية كاملة وقطع مسارات الإمداد اللوجيستي، تمهيداً لمراحل قادمة تهدف لتطويق الجماعة في معاقلها الرئيسة. تشهد ولايات شمال وجنوب وغرب كردفان تصعيداً جوياً عنيفاً من قبل مقاتلات ومسيرات الجيش لتوفير غطاء لتحركاته البرية. ونجحت القوات المسلحة في إعادة تموضعها في عدة جبهات استراتيجية مثل أبو زعيمة وأم بادر، مع تعزيز انتشارها في محاور العمليات بغرب كردفان. في إقليم دارفور، واصلت مسيرات الجيش لليوم السادس غاراتها على مواقع الدعم السريع في مدينة نيالا، مستهدفة مراكز القيادة والسيطرة. وأكدت مصادر ميدانية تدمير مقار لنظم المعلومات ومخازن إمداد، مما أسفر عن مقتل عدد من العناصر والقيادات التابعة للجماعة. تعد مدينة نيالا مركزاً رئيساً للدعم السريع منذ السيطرة عليها في أكتوبر 2023، حيث تُستخدم لاستقبال الإمدادات عبر مطارها الدولي. وقد امتدت الهجمات الجوية لتشمل مدن الفاشر والضعين والجنينة، بالإضافة إلى مناطق حدودية بين ولايتي جنوب كردفان وشرق دارفور. في المقابل، قالت مصادر محلية إن قوات الدعم السريع كثفت هجماتها بالمسيرات على مناطق خسرتها في شمال كردفان. واستهدفت هذه الهجمات مرافق مدنية في مدينة أم روابة، من بينها حافلات ركاب كانت تنتظر التزود بالوقود، دون وقوع إصابات بشرية. تعاني مدينة أم روابة من تدهور حاد في الأوضاع الإنسانية ونقص في السلع الأساسية نتيجة الاستهداف المتكرر للطرق الحيوية. ودانت السلطات المحلية في شمال كردفان هذه الهجمات، واصفة إياها بأنها تستهدف ترويع المدنيين وحرمانهم من الخدمات الضرورية. على صعيد محور النيل الأزرق، تتواصل عمليات السيطرة المتبادلة في المناطق الحدودية مع إثيوبيا، وتحديداً في محيط محافظتي الكرمك وقيسان. وبث عناصر من الجيش مقاطع مصورة تؤكد تحقيق تقدم ميداني جديد في بلدات مدل وبلبوم وخور حسن شمال شرقي الكرمك. استرد الجيش السوداني منطقتي بكوري وأوكليلي بعد مواجهات عنيفة مع قوات الدعم السريع وحلفائها من الحركة الشعبية - شمال. وفتح قائد الفرقة الرابعة مشاة الباب أمام العناصر المسلحة للعودة والانضمام للجيش، مستفيدين من قرار العفو العام المعلن. إنسانياً، حذرت المنسقية العامة لمعسكرات النازحين من تداعيات تقليص برنامج الأغذية العالمي لمساعداته نتيجة نقص التمويل الدولي. وأوضحت المنسقية أن هذا القرار يهدد حياة مئات الآلاف الذين يعانون من سوء التغذية الحاد وتدهور سبل العيش بسبب الحرب والجفاف. صنف مؤشر الجوع العالمي لعام 2026 السودان ضمن الدول التي تواجه مستويات مقلقة من انعدام الأمن الغذائي. وتشير البيانات إلى أن نسبة التقزم بين الأطفال دون الخامسة بلغت 35.4%، بينما يعاني نحو 18.1% من الهزال نتيجة النقص الحاد في الغذاء. حذر شركاء دوليون، بينهم الولايات المتحدة والاتحاد الأوروبي، من احتمال وقوع مجاعة وشيكة في السودان خلال الأشهر المقبلة. وطالب البيان المشترك أطراف النزاع بإزالة العوائق البيروقراطية والأمنية لضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية إلى 19.5 مليون شخص محتاج. في الإطار الدبلوماسي، بحث مستشار البيت الأبيض مسعد بولس مع نائب وزير الخارجية السعودي وليد الخريجي سبل حماية المدنيين. وتناولت المشاورات خيارات البناء على جهود الآلية الرباعية لإيجاد مخرج سياسي ينهي الحرب الدائرة في البلاد. دلالات السودان الجيش السوداني الدعم السريع دارفور كردفان الأزمة الإنسانية شارك المرتبطة بالعمل العام كافيين لضمان الاستقرار المعيشي. أدى نزوح الملايين وتعطل المؤسسات الرسمية وتأخر صرف الرواتب إلى دفع الغالبية للبحث عن بدائل توفر مرونة أكبر وقدرة على التكيف مع الظروف المتغيرة. أفادت مصادر متخصصة في علم الاجتماع الاقتصادي بأن الوظيفة الحكومية كانت تمثل في السابق أداة للتخطيط الاجتماعي والمستقبلي للأسر السودانية، حتى مع محدودية الدخل. إلا أن الأزمة الحالية فرضت واقعاً جديداً جعل من تعدد مصادر الدخل استراتيجية ضرورية للبقاء، بدلاً من الاعتماد الكلي على جهة تشغيل واحدة قد تتوقف في أي لحظة. يرى باحثون أن انتشار العمل الحر والمشاريع الصغيرة لا يعني بالضرورة فقدان التقدير للعمل المؤسسي، بل يعكس تحول الوظيفة إلى مجرد أداة ضمن مجموعة أدوات لتأمين المستقبل. الحرب أثرت بشكل مباشر على الارتباط المكاني بالوظيفة، حيث بات النازحون مضطرين للبحث عن مصادر دخل تتناسب مع مواقعهم الجديدة بعيداً عن مقار عملهم الأصلية. تشير المصادر إلى أن الأجيال الشابة هي الأكثر استعداداً لتبني نماذج عمل غير تقليدية، نظراً لدخولها سوق العمل في بيئة اقتصادية مضطربة أصلاً. هذا الجيل بات يرى في المهارات التقنية والأعمال المستقلة خياراً واقعياً يوفر دخلاً قد يفوق الرواتب الحكومية التي تآكلت قيمتها الشرائية بفعل التضخم والأزمة الاقتصادية. بات التوجه نحو التجارة الإلكترونية وتقديم الخدمات المهنية عبر الإنترنت يمثل طوق نجاة للكثيرين، حيث تتيح التكنولوجيا تجاوز الحدود الجغرافية والوصول إلى أسواق خارجية. ومع ذلك، يواجه هذا النوع من العمل تحديات تقنية ولوجستية تتعلق باستقرار شبكات الاتصال والكهرباء، فضلاً عن صعوبات استلام المدفوعات المالية في ظل تعطل النظام المصرفي. أكد خبراء في سوق العمل أن التحول نحو العمل الحر ينقل جزءاً من المخاطر الاقتصادية إلى العامل نفسه، حيث يفتقر المستقلون إلى التأمينات الاجتماعية والإجازات المدفوعة. ورغم أن العمل المستقل يمنح مساحة لزيادة الدخل، إلا أنه يظل غير مستقر مقارنة بالوظيفة التقليدية التي كانت توفر حداً أدنى من الأمان الوظيفي والمعاشي. في الأسواق المحلية، برزت المشاريع الصغيرة كبديل حيوي لانتظار الوظائف المفقودة، حيث بدأ شباب في إطلاق أنشطة تجارية برؤوس أموال محدودة تشمل مجالات الصيانة والنقل وإعداد الطعام. هذه المشاريع تمنح أصحابها قدرة أكبر على التحكم في قراراتهم الاقتصادية وتعديل نشاطهم بحسب احتياجات السوق المتغيرة في ظل الحرب. تواجه المشاريع الناشئة تحديات جسيمة تتعلق بنقص التمويل وارتفاع تكاليف التشغيل والنقل، بالإضافة إلى تراجع القوة الشرائية للمواطنين. وتلعب الروابط الأسرية دوراً محورياً في دعم هذه الأنشطة من خلال توفير رأس المال الأولي أو المساهمة في الإنتاج، مما يحول المشروع الفردي أحياناً إلى مصدر دخل عائلي مشترك. أوضحت مصادر في الموارد البشرية أن مفهوم الاستقرار المهني لدى الشباب السوداني بات يرتبط الآن بالقدرة على التطور المهني وامتلاك مهارات قابلة للتصدير. لم يعد الحلم محصوراً في مكتب وراتب شهري، بل امتد ليشمل الرغبة في تحقيق دخل بالعملات الأجنبية أو بناء مسار مهني يتيح العمل من أي مكان داخل السودان أو خارجه. الجمع بين الوظيفة الرسمية والعمل الخاص أصبح نموذجاً شائعاً لتقليل الاعتماد على مصدر واحد وتوزيع المخاطر المالية. هذا التوجه يتطلب جهداً مضاعفاً وقدرة عالية على إدارة الوقت، لكنه يمنح الشباب شعوراً بالأمان في حال تعطل أحد المصادر نتيجة الظروف الأمنية أو السياسية المتقلبة في البلاد. يرى مراقبون أن استدامة التحول نحو العمل الحر تتطلب بيئة قانونية ومالية داعمة تشمل التدريب المهني وتسهيل وسائل الدفع الإلكتروني. فبدون هذه المقومات، قد يظل العمل المستقل مجرد صورة من صور العمل غير المنظم الذي لا يوفر حماية حقيقية للعاملين فيه أو قدرة على التخطيط طويل الأمد. تظل جاذبية الوظيفة الحكومية مرتبطة بمدى قدرة الدولة على إصلاح المنظومة الإدارية وانتظام صرف الرواتب وتحسين القدرة الشرائية. وفي حال استمرار الأزمات الحالية، فإن الاعتماد على العمل المرن وتعدد الأنشطة الاقتصادية سيترسخ كسمة أساسية لسوق العمل السوداني في المرحلة المقبلة. إن التغير في عقلية الشباب تجاه العمل ليس مجرد عزوف عن المؤسسات، بل هو محاولة جادة للتكيف مع واقع اقتصادي فرضته الحرب. البحث عن المهارة بدلاً من المنصب يعكس وعياً جديداً بضرورة امتلاك أدوات إنتاج شخصية لا ترتبط بجهة معينة، مما يعزز من مرونة المجتمع في مواجهة الصدمات الاقتصادية. ختاماً، يمثل واقع العمل في السودان اليوم مختبراً للتحولات الاجتماعية والاقتصادية العميقة، حيث يعيد الشباب تعريف النجاح المهني بعيداً عن القوالب التقليدية. تظل المهارة والقدرة على الابتكار هي العملة ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Elevates Sea Access to Existential Security Issue Skip to content October, 2026 Birr Metrics News Feature Insights Interview Startups Editorial Digital Magazine Search for: Search Search Birr Metrics News Feature Insights Interview Startups Editorial Digital Magazine Ethiopia Elevates Sea Access to Existential Security Issue at Tana Forum Amanuel Kindeya October 24, 2026 Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed links Ethiopia’s dependence on foreign ports to national sovereignty, regional security and trade competitiveness as African leaders debate economic independence and geopolitical transformation. Ethiopia has renewed its diplomatic push for access to the sea, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (PhD) describing maritime access as an existential issue affecting the country’s long-term security, economic sovereignty and ability to participate in international trade. Addressing the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa in Bahir Dar on October 24, 2026, Abiy placed Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions within a wider continental discussion about economic independence, regional integration and Africa’s position in a changing geopolitical order. The Prime Minister said Ethiopia, a country of more than 130 million people, faces long-term strategic and economic constraints because its international trade routes pass through neighbouring countries. He maintained that Ethiopia would continue pursuing maritime access through dialogue and arrangements based on mutual benefit, presenting the issue as both a national security priority and an economic development concern. The remarks come as Ethiopia seeks to diversify its external trade routes, reduce dependence on the Djibouti corridor and negotiate more reliable access to international shipping networks. Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, ending its direct access to the Red Sea through Assab and Massawa. The country subsequently developed a heavy dependence on Djibouti, which now handles more than 90 percent of its international merchandise trade. Djibouti’s port infrastructure, connected to Ethiopia by road and the Addis Ababa–Djibouti railway, serves as the country’s principal international trade gateway. The corridor supports imports of petroleum, machinery, industrial inputs and consumer goods, as well as exports of coffee, manufactured products and other commodities. This concentration means disruptions involving port operations, transport infrastructure, border procedures or regional security can affect Ethiopian importers, exporters and domestic supply chains. The financial implications extend beyond port charges. Importers and exporters incur costs associated with inland transportation, customs clearance, container handling, storage and cargo delivery between Djibouti and inland logistics facilities such as Modjo. The government has repeatedly identified high logistics costs and lengthy cargo-processing procedures as constraints on Ethiopia’s manufacturing competitiveness and export development. The maritime question has also become a major diplomatic issue in the Horn of Africa. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland concerning access to the coast. The agreement triggered opposition from Somalia, which considers Somaliland part of its sovereign territory, and led to a diplomatic dispute between Addis Ababa and Mogadishu. The two countries subsequently signed the Ankara Declaration on December 11, 2024, following mediation by Türkiye. Under the declaration, Ethiopia and Somalia reaffirmed respect for each other’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity while acknowledging the potential economic benefits of Ethiopia obtaining reliable access to the sea. The agreement envisaged mutually beneficial commercial arrangements, including contracts and leases, that would provide Ethiopia with secure and sustainable maritime access under Somalia’s sovereign authority. The declaration established a diplomatic framework for negotiations but did not itself grant Ethiopia a port or sovereign maritime territory. Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions also intersect with wider competition in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where strategic shipping routes connect the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal. Djibouti hosts foreign military facilities operated by several countries, including the United States, China, France and Japan. The wider maritime region has also faced security disruptions affecting international shipping, increasing attention to the reliability of trade routes. Against this background, Abiy linked Ethiopia’s position to the broader African challenge of securing predictable access to markets. He said transport corridors and more efficient cross-border arrangements were essential to enabling African producers to reach regional and international buyers. The issue is closely connected to the African Continental Free Trade Area, which aims to expand trade among African economies through tariff reductions, improved market access and measures addressing non-tariff barriers. For landlocked economies, implementing continental trade agreements also depends on transport infrastructure, customs cooperation and access to ports in neighbouring countries. The 12th Tana Forum, held from October 23 to 25 under the theme “Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation,” brings together African leaders, policymakers, researchers and representatives of regional institutions. Its agenda examines how control over economic resources, financial systems, trade networks and strategic infrastructure affects national sovereignty and the continent’s capacity to maintain peace. Abiy also presented Ethiopia’s domestic development and governance philosophy, Medemer, meaning synergy, as part of his wider argument for cooperation and collective African action. The Prime Minister has developed the concept through a series of publications addressing national unity, cooperation and economic transformation, and has increasingly connected it to regional and Pan-African priorities. The Tana Forum was established in 2012 by the Institute for Peace and Security Studies at Addis Ababa University, following the African Union’s 2009 Tripoli Declaration calling for African-led approaches to peace and security. It serves as an informal diplomatic and policy platform bringing together current and former African leaders, regional organisations, researchers and civil society representatives. The 2026 gathering is expected to involve around 250 participants and is examining economic sovereignty, resource governance, regional integration, institutional capacity and the effects of geopolitical competition on African security. Unlike formal African Union summits, the Tana Forum does not negotiate binding agreements. Its discussions are intended to inform policy debates and decision-making within African institutions. In an article published on Megatopia, Professor Al Mariam analyzed historical remarks made by Eritrean President Isaias Afewerki during a press conference in the early 1990s, noting that Egypt and Eritrea have historically coordinated to deprive Ethiopia of peace and generate continuous internal hardship. Al Mariam said the underlying strategic objective binding the axis is securing Egyptian dominance over the Nile waters. He explained that Egyptian political strategy relies on keeping upstream Nile Basin nations in a state of perpetual turmoil to restrict their ability to carry out vital riverine development projects along the Abay River. According to the analyst, President Isaias’ explicit acknowledgment of the campaign to "give Ethiopia work" reflects a deliberate strategy of exhaustion. By fomenting internal conflicts, funding armed insurgent groups, and conducting cross-border military incursions, the axis aims to force the Ethiopian government into continuous defense spending. This systematic diversion of national resources away from socio-economic and infrastructure projects serves to weaken state institutions and undermine national unity, the analyst elaborated. Al Mariam emphasized that the Eritrean regime effectively functions as a client state and proxy for Cairo, carrying out actions that compromise the stability of the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea corridor. He added that the calculated acts of destabilization orchestrated by Egypt and Eritrea constitute a grave threat not only to Ethiopia's sovereignty but also to the broader peace and security of the entire region. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov told Russia’s Izvestia newspaper that Moscow is “ready to provide a platform for organizing contacts between their representatives in order to find compromise solutions,” including at the third Russia-Africa Summit scheduled for October 28-29 in Moscow. He expressed hope that both Ethiopia and Eritrea would take advantage of the opportunity. Alimov said the deterioration of relations between the two countries is a source of concern for Russia, which considers both nations long-standing and reliable partners. The Russian diplomat called on both sides to exercise restraint, strengthen confidence-building measures, and resolve their differences through dialogue and diplomacy. Eritrea Accuses Abiy of Pursuing War for Sea Access Eritrea’s Information Minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, has accused Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed of waging a war of aggression against Eritrea, arguing that Ethiopia’s pursuit of direct Red Sea access poses a threat to Eritrea’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Gebremeskel cited remarks Abiy made to parliament in October 2023, in which the Ethiopian leader stated his intention to secure “sovereign access to the sea, through negotiations if possible and by force if necessary.” Eritrea views this as a direct threat to its port of Assab and a pretext for territorial expansion. In a letter to the UN Security Council, Eritrea requested that the council “forcefully condemn Ethiopia’s deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea” and take “requisite deterrent measures” under Chapter VII of the UN Charter. Eritrea’s Foreign Minister, Osman Saleh, warned that the Ethiopian action would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilize the whole region.” Ethiopia responded with its own letter to the Security Council, invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter and accusing Eritrea of deploying infantry and mechanized units across the border and supporting, financing, arming, and directing insurgent groups. Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described Eritrea’s actions as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence.” Ethiopia’s Naval Expansion and the Red Sea Gambit The crisis is rooted in Ethiopia’s determination to re-establish a naval presence and secure direct access to the Red Sea, a goal that has intensified under Abiy’s government. Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and the country has repeatedly insisted that its “legitimate interests” in the Red Sea must be recognized. Ethiopia’s naval chief, Deputy Admiral Kindu Gezu, has acknowledged that the country’s naval force is being expanded from “zero,” with investments in training, infrastructure, and specialized combat units aimed at protecting national interests and responding to security challenges. The naval expansion comes as Ethiopia seeks to position itself as a maritime player in the Red Sea, despite not having a direct coastline. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Abiy’s Red Sea strategy , the Ethiopian Prime Minister has explicitly linked durable peace in the Horn of Africa to Ethiopia obtaining direct sea access, arguing that the absence of ports restricts the country’s economic expansion and international competitiveness. The Somaliland Option Despite its naval ambitions and its January 2024 memorandum of understanding with Somaliland that reportedly traded possible recognition for coastal access, Ethiopia has stopped short of formal recognition. The reason, according to Ethiopia’s Ambassador to Israel, Tesfaye Yetayeh Anteneh, is the risk of triggering a security collapse in Somalia. “The moment, for example, Ethiopia recognizes Somaliland, the Somali government will request Ethiopia to withdraw its troops from Somalia,” Anteneh said in an interview with i24NEWS. “And Al-Shabaab will get a free ride to attack both Somalia and Somaliland, even a spillover effect will come also to Ethiopia”. The ambassador described recognition as “a very delicate issue” and said Ethiopia “shouldn’t rush” into a decision that could unravel the security arrangement that keeps Ethiopian troops deployed in Somalia under the African Union mission. Ethiopia has been a central troop contributor in Somalia since 2006 and currently serves in the new African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which began operating in January 2025. Anteneh’s explanation reveals a strategic calculation that treats recognition less as a question of principle than as a sequencing problem. Ethiopia wants sea access. It sees Somaliland as a potential pathway. But it also depends on cooperation with Mogadishu to maintain its military presence and combat Al-Shabaab. Recognition, at this juncture, would jeopardize that cooperation without guaranteeing the benefits. Somaliland’s ambassador to Israel, Mohamed Hagi, rejected this reasoning, arguing that recognition would strengthen Ethiopia’s security rather than undermine it, and that Mogadishu’s growing alignment with Ethiopia’s rivals posed a greater strategic threat. Somalia’s Parallel Fear: The Same Threat, A Different Border Eritrea’s alarm over Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions is not unique. Somalia shares the same fundamental fear, having already experienced what Eritrea now anticipates. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Somaliland, the breakaway region Somalia considers its territory, granting Addis Ababa access to a 20-kilometer coastal strip at the port of Berbera for 50 years in exchange for potential recognition of Somaliland’s independence. Somalia rejected the agreement as a “blatant violation” of its sovereignty. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud described the deal as “nothing more than annexing part of Somalia to Ethiopia, and changing the borders of Somalia.” A Somali diplomat, speaking privately, put it more starkly: “This is not a port deal. This is a question of our existence as a nation.” As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Ethiopia’s Somaliland strategy , Addis Ababa has carefully positioned itself to move toward recognition without becoming diplomatically isolated. But the ambassador’s recent remarks suggest that the calculation is more complex than a simple trade of recognition for port access. The Ankara Declaration, brokered by Türkiye in December 2025, eased the immediate crisis by reaffirming both countries’ commitment to each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity while acknowledging Ethiopia’s interest in reliable sea access through commercial arrangements under Somali sovereignty. But the underlying tension remains unresolved. President Mohamud has said Somalia is open to Ethiopia using Somali ports, but only through direct negotiations with Mogadishu and under Somali sovereignty. For Somalia, the Eritrea-Ethiopia crisis is therefore not a distant dispute. It is a mirror image of its own confrontation with Addis Ababa, playing out on a different border. Eritrea’s accusation that Ethiopia is pursuing war to secure sea access echoes Mogadishu’s own experience with the Somaliland MoU . And Eritrea’s warning that Ethiopia’s actions could “destabilize the whole region” is a warning Somalia has already lived through. The Alamein Coalition and Its Fractures The Eritrea-Ethiopia standoff directly affects Somalia because both countries are signatories to the El Alamein Joint Declaration, signed on October 4, 2026, by Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, and Somalia. That declaration formalized coordination on regional security, affirmed respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and stated that the management of the Red Sea is a responsibility exclusive to its littoral states. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the standoff , two of Somalia’s four partners in that declaration are now on the brink of war with each other, fracturing a coalition that was designed to present a united front against Ethiopian regional ambitions and Israeli recognition of Somaliland. The declaration explicitly rejected recognition of Somaliland and affirmed that Red Sea governance is the exclusive responsibility of littoral states, a provision clearly aimed at Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions. But with Eritrea and Ethiopia now exchanging accusations of aggression, the coalition’s ability to act collectively is severely compromised. Somalia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Hassan Mohamed Ali Nadar has said Mogadishu remains neutral in the Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute, maintaining relations with both countries and supporting peaceful solutions . That neutrality is pragmatic but precarious. Somalia has cultivated close relationships with both Egypt and Eritrea, viewing them as partners in its own domestic security appratus. But Somalia also relies on Ethiopia for security cooperation and troop contributions to the African Union mission. The prospect of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war places Mogadishu in an impossible position, forced to choose between regional partners whose conflict it cannot influence. Critical Note Russia’s offer to mediate is a diplomatic gesture that reflects Moscow’s desire to remain relevant in the Horn of Africa, where it has cultivated relationships with both Addis Ababa and Asmara. But mediation requires willing parties, and neither Ethiopia nor Eritrea has publicly accepted the offer or indicated readiness to compromise on the core issue: Ethiopia’s demand for Red Sea access and Eritrea’s determination to defend its sovereignty. The deeper problem is that the Eritrea-Ethiopia crisis is not a bilateral dispute that can be resolved through talks in Moscow. It is a structural collision between Ethiopia’s landlocked geography and its great-power ambitions, on one hand, and Eritrea’s insistence on the inviolability of its borders, on the other. Russia can provide a venue. It cannot provide a solution. For Somalia, the crisis is both a warning and a mirror. The Alamein Declaration was signed less than three weeks ago. Two (Eritrea an Sudan) of its signatories are now publicly throwing accusations. Somalia’s own confrontation with Ethiopia over the Somaliland MoU remains unresolved, and the same logic that drives Eritrea’s fears drives Mogadishu’s. Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access has already destabilized one border in the Horn. It now threatens to destabilize another. The Ethiopian ambassador’s explanation for why recognition is on hold is a reminder that Addis Ababa’s restraint is tactical, not principled. It depends on the costs of recognition remaining high. Somalia’s diplomatic strategy of aligning with Egypt and Eritrea against Ethiopian expansionism is understandable, but it depends on partners who are themselves locked in conflict. In the Horn of Africa, partnerships are provisional, and the only constant is the region’s capacity for sudden, destabilizing change. Share your story. Kindiki was received at Bahir Dar International Airport on Saturday by Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The forum, running from October 23 to 25, brings together African leaders, policymakers and other stakeholders to discuss the continent’s peace and security challenges under the theme, “Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation.” Discussions will examine how Africa’s management of its resources, economic institutions and regional integration can contribute to lasting peace. According to the organisers, the agenda includes resource wealth and monetary sovereignty for industrial development, macroeconomic governance, and the impact of illicit economies on regional stability. About 250 participants are expected, including sitting and former heads of state and government, diplomats, academics, civil society representatives and private sector leaders. Organised by the Institute for Peace and Security Studies at Addis Ababa University, the Tana Forum provides an informal platform for leaders and experts to debate African-led responses to security challenges. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Strategic Interests, Historic Ties Bind It to Red Sea: Ambassador Zerihun - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia’s Strategic Interests, Historic Ties Bind It to Red Sea: Ambassador Zerihun - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia’s Strategic Interests, Historic Ties Bind It to Red Sea: Ambassador Zerihun 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 24, 2026 (ENA) —Ethiopia’s strategic importance, historical ties, and geographic realities make its connection to the Red Sea inseparable from its national interests, Director General for African Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Zerihun Abebe said. Briefing journalists on the sidelines of the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa in Bahir Dar, Ambassador Zerihun underscored that Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access is rooted in history, geography, and national security. “We have repeatedly stated that the issue of a sea outlet is a matter of survival for Ethiopia,” he said, adding that the country has developed policy strategies to advance this objective. He stressed that Ethiopia cannot be excluded from discussions on the Red Sea, given its strategic position, security interests, and role in the wider region. The evolving regional realities, he added, call for cooperation that takes Ethiopia’s interests into account. Ambassador Zerihun reaffirmed Ethiopia’s commitment to working with regional countries to advance peace, development, and shared security, describing the Tana Forum as an important platform for strengthening cooperation and addressing common challenges. He also emphasized the need for a regional anchor capable of contributing to peace, development, and stability, asserting that Ethiopia has historically played—and continues to play—such a role. The remarks come as regional and international stakeholders gather in Bahir Dar for the Tana Forum’s Special Envoys’ Dialogue, which is examining the evolving geopolitics of the Horn of Africa and mounting security challenges in the Red Sea. In his welcoming remarks, National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS), Director General Redwan Hussein highlighted the strategic importance of the Red Sea and its maritime trade routes, warning that growing militarization, competition among external powers, and attacks on commercial shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait pose risks to regional stability. He emphasized that securing the Red Sea requires collective action by regional states and reliable international partners. He noted that Ethiopia has significant stake in maritime security as a country dependent on the Red Sea for its international trade. High-level discussions under the theme: “Regional Security in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea” brought together African and international envoys to examine the region’s changing security and geopolitical landscape. Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Ethiopia-style guerrilla insurgencies could emerge in Somalia: official Ethiopia-style guerrilla insurgencies could emerge in Somalia: official October 24, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia could face the emergence of Ethiopia-style guerrilla factions in several regions as political rivalries deepen and competing power centres reportedly seek military backing, former Somali intelligence chief Abdirahman Turyare warned on Friday. Turyare, who currently serves as Somalia’s envoy to the Islamic Military Counter-Terrorism Coalition, cautioned that armed movements resembling those operating in Ethiopia’s Tigray, Amhara and Oromia regions could emerge in Somalia, particularly in Hiran, Middle Shabelle and Bay. He warned that the potential factions could eventually forge alliances with Al-Shabaab, the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group waging an insurgency against Somalia’s federal government, and urged authorities to prevent their emergence before they develop into a broader security threat. Turyare also issued a stark warning to those allegedly seeking to establish the armed factions, cautioning them against gambling with their lives by pursuing a course that could plunge the country into further violence. His remarks come amid growing reports in Somali local media suggesting that political disputes between Mogadishu and regional power brokers are increasingly intersecting with allegations of external military support and preparations for new armed formations. Sanbalolshe reportedly seeks military backing in Ethiopia At the centre of the latest concerns is former Somali intelligence chief Abdullahi Mohamed Ali Sanbalolshe, who, according to local media reports, is in the border town of Ferfer to receive military support from Ethiopia. The reports allege that Sanbalolshe intends to establish a powerful armed force capable of wresting control of the entire Hiran region from the federal government. His reported plans come against the backdrop of a growing political dispute involving his Hawadle clan and Mogadishu over the leadership of the Hirshabelle regional administration. The disagreement centres on the selection of the region’s president. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud backed Ali Gudlawe, who belongs to his own clan, for the position. Gudlawe was re-elected on Saturday, further intensifying the political tensions surrounding the regional leadership contest. The allegations concerning Sanbalolshe’s movements, military support and reported plans have not been independently verified. Middle Shabelle tensions and alleged UAE support A separate set of local media reports points to possible preparations for another armed faction in neighbouring Middle Shabelle. Abdullahi Mohamed Nur, a wealthy businessman affiliated with the clan of opposition leader Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, is reportedly planning to establish a guerrilla force in the region, allegedly with military support from the United Arab Emirates. The reports further claim that Nur possesses a substantial number of Ma’awisley fighters drawn from his own clan. Ma’awisley forces are locally organised armed groups that have played a significant role in Somalia’s fight against Al-Shabaab, particularly in central regions. Their potential mobilisation amid political disputes could add another layer of complexity to an already fragile security environment. The allegations of planned military assistance from the UAE, like those concerning Ethiopia, remain unverified. Bay remains a flashpoint after Laftagareen’s ouster The warnings come as Somalia’s federal government continues to grapple with guerrilla warfare by forces loyal to former Southwest State leader Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. Laftagareen was ousted from power in March by a military operation, forcing his forces out of Baidoa, the interim regional capital. Since then, his fighters have shifted to guerrilla tactics, challenging federal authority across the region. According to the reports, Laftagareen’s forces made significant territorial gains last week, retaking five districts across Bay region, leaving Baidoa as the only town in the region outside their control. The renewed fighting underscores the difficulties facing the federal government as it attempts to consolidate its authority following the change of leadership in Southwest State. The developments also raise concerns that political confrontations, if increasingly pursued through armed proxies and irregular forces, could open additional fronts in a country already fighting a protracted insurgency. Fears of a wider security crisis The Somali federal government has not yet publicly commented on the reports concerning the alleged formation of new guerrilla factions, the purported external military backing or Turyare’s warning. The reports have nevertheless emerged amid mounting political tensions across Somalia, fuelling concerns that disputes between Mogadishu and its opponents could escalate into a wider cycle of armed confrontation. The potential consequences extend beyond individual regional power struggles. The emergence of additional armed factions in Hiran, Middle Shabelle and Bay could complicate counterterrorism operations, weaken federal authority and create opportunities for Al-Shabaab to exploit divisions among political and clan-based rivals. Turyare’s warning highlights the risk that armed groups established to advance political or regional interests could eventually become part of a more fragmented security landscape, particularly if they develop relationships with established militant organisations. For Somalia, the prospect of simultaneous conflicts involving federal forces, regional factions, clan-based militias and al-Shabaab presents a serious challenge at a time when the country continues to depend on extensive international political, financial and security support. Somalia has spent years rebuilding state institutions and security structures following decades of conflict and state collapse. A further spread of politically driven armed violence could undermine those gains, deepen regional instability and threaten the fragile process of state-building that has continued since 2004. Privacy Policy Terms of Service Search GSEF 2026: Somalia's Ambassador to Kenya Says Somali Investors Are Tried and Tested October 24, 2026 5 min read HW By - Editor Hassan Wekesa Kenya, 24 October 2026 - Somalia’s Ambassador to Kenya, Jabril Ibrahim Abdulle, has hailed the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum (GSEF) as a platform that connects investors and businesses across the region, noting that trade improvements are evident. Speaking at the forum, now in its third year, he said remittances from the diaspora should go beyond consumption and be channelled into investment ventures back home, in the East Africa region and elsewhere where business environment is conducive. He noted that the forum continues to bring together investors, and that the eight member states of the East African Community (EAC) have a combined population of around 300 million people. The EAC member states are Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, South Sudan, and Somalia. “Trade improvements are evident,” Ambassador Abdulle said at the Radisson Blu Hotel, Upper Hill, Nairobi, adding that networks connect businesses. He urged the Somali diaspora to keep working hard and not to worry about how long they have stayed away from home. To him, what counts is the remittances that enable those back home to invest in various ventures rather than simply consume. “A man is judged by what he or she brings home, not necessarily how long he or she has stayed away,” Ambassador Abdulle said. He said the forum comes hot on the heels of both Kenyan and Somali leaders attending the 25th Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe. He added that Kenya and Somalia share a lot in common, and that the relationship between the two neighbouring countries remains strong and warm. Ambassador Abdulle also said that envoys from many countries ask him how they can attract Somali investors, because “our people have been tried and tested.” Entrepreneurs Still Face Challenges Other speakers at GSEF 2026 said that while the Somali community is known to thrive in entrepreneurial ventures, both back home and in the diaspora, many businesses still encounter enormous challenges. Dr Ahmednur Abdi, the Chief Policy Advisor and former Permanent Secretary in the Office of the Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Somalia, said entrepreneurs need simpler regulations and simpler dispute resolution mechanisms, among other interventions. He noted that, without any iota of doubt, the Somali people are resilient. “We should move from survival to reach potential. Somali innovation is visible,” he said. Dr Abdi urged both governments and investors to improve services and infrastructure. “We must ensure that the technologies we have help farmers, for instance, to reach markets,” he stated. Delegates follow proceedings during the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum (GSEF) 2026 at the Radisson Blu Hotel, Upper Hill, Nairobi, on Saturday, 24 October 2026. Photo: Dawan Africa He also called for collaboration between countries, their citizens and businesspeople so that they can tackle serious questions such as “can goods cross boundaries without delay?” Targeted investments in roads, energy and logistics, he said, would help streamline thriving business activity in the East African region. He urged governments in EAC member states to provide clear regulations. However, Dr Abdi challenged the Federal Government of Somalia to wake up from its slumber, arguing that the private sector in Somalia was doing much better and that “the Government must keep at par with the private sector.” More from Kenya CS Aden Duale Jokes Somalia Has Many Gachaguas At GSEF 2026 Event in Nairobi Somalia’s Electoral Commission Announces Candidates for Hirshabelle State Leader and Deputy Dr Abdi is a seasoned governance and policy expert with more than 25 years of experience. He was glad to bring to the forum his deep expertise in public-sector reform, federalism, institutional development and lessons from post-conflict recovery. He established Somalia’s first Directors General Forum and has led the Federal Negotiation Technical Committee (FNTC), which brings together representatives of the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS) and the Federal Member States (FMS) to support negotiations on key federalism matters. He later led the State Formation Committee for the Northwest Somalia State. Duale: Somalia Must Find Political Goodwill The Chief Guest at the forum was Kenya’s Health Cabinet Secretary, Aden Duale, who said that people who do not know Somali business acumen and agility “take us for granted.” He said the time was ripe for Somalis back in the Federal Republic of Somalia to shape the destiny of their nation, because what is lacking there is political goodwill. “Countries that went under at the same time as Somalia are back on their feet. It is sad that 30 years later, Somalia still faces the same political fragility,” he said. He said many politicians in Somalia are his friends, but they must start thinking about how the country can turn around instead of burying their heads in the sand when it is supposed to sprout and grow. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale addresses delegates as Chief Guest at the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum 2026 on Saturday, 24 October 2026. Photo: Dawan Africa He thanked the GSEF secretariat for offering the platform to investors, innovators and policymakers, among other stakeholders. He said that what counts now is for the platform to translate into practical opportunities, where entrepreneurs meet clients and strike meaningful business deals. “What matters now is not how many people attend this forum, but the business deals entrepreneurs get out of this distinguished gathering,” CS Duale stated. He said East Africa is at a critical moment, with countries still grappling with youth unemployment, poor infrastructure and other bottlenecks that bedevil the region. “The potential of our people can be tapped to realise full potential. We must create stronger pathways for entrepreneurs,” CS Duale said. He advised Somalia to follow in the footsteps of other EAC member states by ratifying all the requirements of the bloc, not just through the Legislative arm. He cited customs as an area the government should streamline if “Somalia wants to experience the business boom we see every day at the Kenya Ports Authority (KPA).” CS Duale said Kenya and Somalia have a strong connection, and that it is therefore important for both countries to enable entrepreneurs to access larger markets. “Government leadership is very important,” he advised. Businesses showcasing at the forum included Takaful Insurance, Beba Fleet, Fly Dubai, Amanah Insurance, BananaPay, Astral Aviation and Roasting Peacock. Abdelaziz Adan Abdullahi explains to attendees of the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum (GSEF) 2026 how BananaPay works. Photo: Dawan Africa Also present were Vickers Security Services Ltd, Aga Khan University, Aga Khan Hospital, Salaam Somali Bank, Travel Takaful, PayOn Time and Silva Gigiri. The two-day forum started on Saturday and ends on Sunday. He urged the Somali diaspora to invest in their homeland rather than merely sending remittances for consumption. Abdulle noted the importance of the East African Community (EAC), which comprises around 300 million people, in fostering trade and business connections. Despite the entrepreneurial spirit within the Somali community, challenges persist, as pointed out by Dr. Ahmednur Abdi, who called for simpler regulations and improved infrastructure to facilitate business operations. The forum showcased various businesses and aimed to create opportunities for meaningful partnerships among entrepreneurs, policymakers, and investors, ultimately seeking to enhance the region's economic landscape.

Privacy Policy Terms of Service Search CS Aden Duale Jokes Somalia Has Many Gachaguas At GSEF 2026 Event in Nairobi | Dawan Africa | Dawan Africa CS Aden Duale Jokes Somalia Has Many Gachaguas At GSEF 2026 Event in Nairobi October 24, 2026 5 min read HW By Hassan Wekesa - Editor Kenya, 24 October 2026 - Kenya’s Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale on Saturday launched a scathing attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua during the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum 2026. Duale, who was the Chief Guest, said Kenyan parliamentarians made the right decision to impeach the former second in command. He claimed Gachagua was sowing seeds of discord in the country. “Just two years after President William Ruto ascended to power, we realised that Kenya could not move forward with Gachagua as the Deputy President,” CS Duale said. He said this as he implored Somalis in the Federal Republic of Somalia to put the right leaders in office when they go to the polls. Duale hailed President Ruto and urged Somalia to be careful about whom it entrusts with the leadership mantle. The Health CS joked that “Somalia currently has so many Gachaguas.” “I can help you identify Gachaguas whether in Somalia or in Uganda,” he claimed. This is not the first time Duale has claimed he can reveal the names of perceived detractors of development. He had earlier threatened to release the names of people who allegedly funded al-Shabaab terrorist activities in Kenya, but he went silent over the promise. Nonetheless, CS Duale’s claim against Gachagua was that he was allegedly interested in “shareholder politics” at a time when President Ruto was keen on achieving equitable development across the country. In just four years, he said, President Ruto has achieved what his four predecessors, Mzee Jomo Kenyatta, Daniel Toroitich arap Moi, Mwai Kibaki and retired President Uhuru Kenyatta, never managed. He said Kenya is currently the seventh largest economy in Africa and the leading one in the East African region, with a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of $151 billion. “Kenya is 10 times ahead of Somalia. In our region, Kenya leads ahead of Ethiopia, Tanzania and Uganda,” he said. He added that, under the able leadership of President Ruto, the Kenya shilling has remained stable against the US dollar. “Kenya Shilling stabilised from KSh 165 per Dollar to KSh 130, which has really stabilised there for over two years,” he said. He said Kenya’s agricultural sector has also improved. On government services, he said, over 7,000 of them can now be accessed through the eCitizen platform. Digitisation of services has also improved access to information, enabling the government to track statistics and plan effectively for the development of its people. He laughed off some Kenyans who label the Somali community as backward. “When some people talk ill about we Somalis, I tell them to go think about it,” he said, adding that Somalis worldwide are agile and risk takers. More from Kenya GSEF 2026: Somalia's Ambassador to Kenya Says Somali Investors Are Tried and Tested Somalia’s Electoral Commission Announces Candidates for Hirshabelle State Leader and Deputy “Here in Kenya and East Africa, everyone knows CJ’s Restaurant, which originated in Uganda but is doing very well here in Kenya,” Duale said. “Somalis are agile, but what they now lack is generational wealth. I urge each one of you attending this forum to go and read the book The Jewish Phenomenon ,” he said. He also cited the Ismaili Muslim community and gave the example of the Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN). Overall, he stated, what countries need to do is collaborate. “Generational wealth is very important. Right now, maybe 10 Somali businesses are generational wealth. Many you find have a restaurant today, and in six months they are trying something to do with cattle. In other words, we need to have generational wealth,” he stated. He argued that families must learn to build generational wealth, where one group is in insurance, another in banking, another in technology, and so on. He also highlighted how, on many occasions during foreign trips as a government official, he bumps into Somalis eking out a living abroad. “I remember we were in Guinea Bissau with President Ruto. He challenged me, thinking that it would be difficult to find a Somali. He dared that if I found any from our community, he would give me KSh 2 million. I found two of them, who told me they coordinate with other Somali diaspora, Egyptians and some Indians to sell cashew nuts,” he said. He added that Somali footprints are found all over. In Lusaka, Zambia, he said, one would think they were in Garissa, Kenya, or Mogadishu, Somalia. He urged Somalis back in Somalia to fix politics there, and the Somali government to ensure that everything is set and that the country ratifies all the requirements of the East African Community (EAC). “Being a member of the Legislative arm alone is not enough. Please ensure the customs are in sync, and that will spur economic activity,” he advised. He was categorical that Kenya and Somalia have a strong connection, and advised that citizens and governments on both sides must do what is needed to ensure a thriving business environment. Businesses showcasing at the forum included Takaful Insurance, Beba Fleet, Fly Dubai, Amanah Insurance, BananaPay, Astral Aviation, and Roasting Peacock. Also present were Vickers Security Services Ltd, Aga Khan University, Aga Khan Hospital, Salaam Somali Bank, Travel Takaful and PayOn Time, and Silva Gigiri. The two-day event ends on Sunday, 25 October 2026. Kenya's Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has urged Somalis to fix politics and ratify EAC requirements fast. Duale, the event's Chief Guest, emphasized the importance of electing capable leaders in Somalia, urging the audience to learn from Kenya’s political experiences. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia condemns deadly attack on church in Jordan Posted by: Horseed Staff Somalia has condemned a deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan’s Karak governorate, expressing solidarity with the Jordanian government and the families of those killed. 24 October, 2026 Share Tweet Eight people were killed and dozens wounded after gunmen opened fire on Friday during a funeral at a church in Hmoud village, about 90km (56 miles) south of the capital, Amman, according to Jordanian authorities. The death toll rose from seven to eight on Saturday after one of those critically injured died in hospital. “The Federal Republic of Somalia strongly condemns the terrorist attack in Karak Governorate, in the brotherly Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, which killed and injured innocent people,” Somalia’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement. “Somalia knows the human cost of terrorism and rejects violence and extremism in all their forms,” the ministry added. Somalia extended its condolences to the families of those killed and wished those injured a speedy recovery. Jordanian authorities have described the shooting as a terrorist attack. Health officials said at least 40 people were wounded, with dozens still receiving treatment on Saturday. Jordan declared three days of national mourning following the attack, with flags ordered to half-staff at government institutions. Authorities have not publicly identified the attackers or announced a motive. Security forces continued efforts to identify and arrest those responsible. King Abdullah II condemned the attack and said those responsible would face justice, while Prime Minister Jafar Hassan described the shooting as an assault on all Jordanians. The attack has drawn condemnation from governments and international organisations across the region and beyond, as authorities continue their investigation into the circumstances and motive behind the shooting. Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud congratulated Mr Gudlawe on his re-election, as well as the newly elected vice-president, Abdifatah Hassan Afrah. The two were elected in Jowhar. President Hassan Sheikh wished the new leadership success and urged them to effectively carry out the responsibilities entrusted to them. He stressed the importance of accelerating efforts to promote peace, reconciliation, state-building and the improvement of public services across Hirshabelle. The president also praised the electoral process through which the new leadership was chosen, highlighting the importance of strengthening democratic institutions, developing state structures and increasing public participation in Somalia’s political process. The Hirshabelle election has also faced controversy over the process by which it was conducted, with opposition from sections of the Hiiraan community who argued that the process did not adequately represent the region. The dispute comes amid wider disagreements over Somalia’s electoral system, with opposition figures accusing the federal government of seeking to extend President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s tenure beyond its scheduled end in May. The government has rejected such criticisms and maintained that its political and electoral efforts are aimed at strengthening the country’s democratic institutions and political process. somalia.summary: Ali Gudlawe Hussein has been re-elected as the president of Hirshabelle State in Somalia, following a vote by 81 lawmakers in Jowhar, the state capital. His re-election was met with congratulations from Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who also welcomed the newly elected vice-president, Abdifatah Hassan Afrah. President Mohamud emphasized the need for the new leadership to focus on peace, reconciliation, state-building, and enhancing public services in Hirshabelle. He praised the electoral process, underscoring the importance of strengthening democratic institutions and increasing public participation in Somalia's political landscape. However, the election has sparked controversy, particularly among segments of the Hiiraan community, who argue that the electoral process did not adequately represent their interests. This dispute occurs against a backdrop of broader tensions regarding Somalia's electoral system, with some opposition figures accusing the federal government of attempting to extend President Mohamud’s term beyond its scheduled end in May. The government has dismissed these allegations, asserting its commitment to democratic development.

Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somaliland journalist detained after interviewing Somalia presidential hopeful Posted by: Horseed Staff A journalist working for Horn Cable TV has been detained by authorities in Somaliland after interviewing a politician who has declared his intention to run for Somalia’s presidency. 24 October, 2026 Share Tweet Journalist Abdirahman Egeh was arrested in Hargeisa on Thursday, days after Somaliland authorities detained Abdikadir Mohamed Sharaay, a politician and academic who announced his presidential ambitions during an interview broadcast by the channel in mid-October. During the interview, Mr Sharaay said he intended to contest Somalia’s presidential election, scheduled for May 2027. He also argued that Somaliland should seek international recognition through negotiations with Somalia’s federal government in Mogadishu, rather than relying on support from Israel and other countries. His comments prompted debate on social media, with some Somaliland politicians and commentators calling for action against him. The circumstances surrounding the two arrests remain unclear. Authorities have not publicly established whether Mr Egeh’s detention was directly linked to the interview or to Mr Sharaay’s subsequent arrest. The detention of Mr Egeh has drawn criticism from journalists and media freedom advocates, who have questioned whether a reporter should face legal consequences for interviewing a person expressing political views. The latest detentions come amid growing criticism of Somaliland authorities over the arrest of journalists following interviews involving political criticism. In August, authorities detained journalist Abdiqani Hussein Abokor, known as Baylood, after an interview on Heegan TV with poet Ismail Yusuf Abdi, known as Jiheeye. During that interview, Mr Jiheeye criticised Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro over a property dispute. Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and has since maintained its own government and security institutions. It has long sought international recognition as an independent state, while its relationship with Mogadishu remains strained over sovereignty, recognition and the territory’s political status. Neither Somaliland’s government nor its security agencies has publicly explained the legal grounds for the arrests of Mr Sharaay and Mr Egeh. It is also unclear whether either man has been formally charged. The celebrations, hosted at the Ugandan embassy in Mogadishu, were attended by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud as chief guest. He congratulated his Ugandan counterpart, Yoweri Museveni, and the people of Uganda, reaffirming the longstanding friendship and partnership between the two nations. President Mohamud paid tribute to the sacrifices of Ugandan troops who have served in Somalia since 2007, when Uganda became the first country to deploy forces under the African Union Mission in Somalia. He recalled President Museveni’s visit to Mogadishu in 1992, at a time of severe insecurity, describing it as an extraordinary demonstration of solidarity with the Somali people. “We will work with you, and Somali institutions will work with you, and you will have what you have requested,” Mohamud told Ugandan business people at the event, pledging his government’s support for their interests. Three Days of Economic Diplomacy The independence celebrations capped a series of engagements that began with the mid-term review of the Uganda-Somalia Joint Permanent Commission and the first-ever Somali-Ugandan Business Forum. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the business forum , it was the first time Mogadishu had hosted a meeting of the commission, which was established in 2022. More than 100 Ugandan delegates and 146 Somali representatives participated in the review, alongside an investment and business forum and a joint exhibition at the Airport Hotel, as reported in Dawan Africa’s coverage of the meetings . Discussions covered security, trade, investment, tourism, labour, aviation, and health cooperation. A bilateral labour agreement was among the documents signed, aimed at regulating the employment of citizens from both countries and protecting workers’ rights. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the labour agreement , the accord establishes a framework for orderly recruitment, outlines employer responsibilities, standardizes contract procedures, and includes protections against abuse and unlawful exploitation. Uganda’s Minister of Gender, Labour and Social Development, Lt. Gen. (Rtd.) Henry Tumukunde, signed the agreement alongside Somalia’s Minister of Labour and Social Affairs, Prof. Salim Alio Ibro. Trade Growth and Untapped Potential The economic dimension of the relationship has grown significantly, though from a low base. Uganda’s exports to Somalia rose from $2.75 million in 2023 to $6.78 million in 2024, according to UN Comtrade data, as reported by The Independent Uganda . Tobacco products led the exports at $2.55 million, followed by aircraft and parts at $1.2 million, and wood products at $528,470. Trade in the opposite direction remains minimal. Somalia exported goods worth $35,400 to Uganda in 2021, down from $671,000 in 2016. “Our imports and exports between Uganda and Somalia have exponentially grown. However, we believe that our private sector can do better than the current statistics,” said Vincent Bagiire Waiswa, Uganda’s Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Bagiire described Somalia as a potential trade bridge between Africa and the Gulf states, noting that Uganda is landlocked while Somalia has Africa’s longest coastline. He described Mogadishu as a prospective “New Dubai” within the East African Community. The EAC Framework Both countries are now members of the East African Community, which Somalia joined in 2024 as its eighth member state. The EAC’s Common Market Protocol provides for the free movement of goods, services, labour, and capital, offering a framework for deeper integration. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Somalia’s EAC membership , the government views regional integration as a mechanism to create opportunities for Somali businesses operating across East Africa. The EAC represents a combined market of over 300 million people. Direct air links have also improved. Uganda Airlines now flies to Mogadishu four times a week, providing the only nonstop connection between Entebbe and the Somali capital. Officials from both countries are pushing to conclude a Bilateral Air Services Agreement to formalize and expand aviation cooperation. Critical Note The three days of engagement in Mogadishu represent a deliberate effort by both governments to broaden a relationship that has historically been defined by security cooperation. Uganda has contributed troops to African Union missions in Somalia for nearly two decades, and President Mohamud’s tribute to their sacrifices was genuine and appropriate. But the economic relationship remains modest. Bilateral trade of less than $7 million annually is negligible for two countries of Somalia’s and Uganda’s size. The Joint Permanent Investment and Business Council agreed in 2025 has not been operationalized. The air services agreement remains unsigned. The memoranda on customs, standards, and health are still drafts. A forum that produces a labour agreement and a communiqué is not the same as a forum that produces trade. The deeper obstacle is not a lack of goodwill. It is the infrastructure and institutional gaps that make commercial exchange costly and unreliable. Uganda Airlines’ four weekly flights are a thin lifeline. Somalia’s ports and customs systems remain weak. And the security partnership that has defined the relationship for two decades is entering an uncertain phase, with the UN Security Council’s authorization for AUSSOM expiring at the end of 2026 and Uganda’s military leadership setting a withdrawal deadline of August 2027. The celebrations in Mogadishu were a moment of friendship and shared purpose. Whether they mark the beginning of a genuine economic partnership, or simply another ceremonial chapter in a security-dominated relationship, will depend on whether the commitments made this week are implemented. The private sector, as Bagiire said, can do better. But it cannot do so without the conditions that allow it to operate. somalia.content: Ismail Mohamed Shines as Somalia's U-15 Cubs Win FIFA Opener Against Puerto Rico - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Sports Nationwide Ismail Mohamed Shines as Somalia’s U-15 Cubs Win FIFA Opener Against Puerto Rico October 24, 2026 5 min read BAKU , Somalia’s Under-15 national football team opened its campaign at the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival with a 3-1 victory over Puerto Rico on Saturday, led by a standout performance from Ismail Mohamed, who was named Man of the Match after scoring two goals and providing one assist. The victory, Somalia’s first at any FIFA tournament, was witnessed by the country’s Ambassador to Azerbaijan, Abdinur Dahir Fidow, who attended the match to support the young players. Mohamed’s contribution accounted for all three of Somalia’s goals, a performance that underlined the forward’s importance to the team’s campaign. For a nation whose football infrastructure has been rebuilt from the ruins of more than three decades of conflict, the moment carried significance beyond the scoreline. The Somali Football Federation described the participation as a historic milestone for the country’s youth program, noting that Somalia had never previously competed in a FIFA World Cup tournament at any age level. Group T: A Competitive Field Somalia has been drawn in Group T alongside Venezuela, Madagascar, Mozambique, Puerto Rico, and New Zealand. The group stage is compressed into a tight schedule, with teams playing multiple matches between October 24 and 26. Somalia’s next match is against Venezuela on Sunday, October 25. Venezuela enters the match with momentum after a 5-0 victory over New Zealand in their opening fixture. The result will be crucial in determining Somalia’s placement within the tournament’s unique tier system. A Tournament Unlike Any Other The inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival is unlike any previous FIFA competition. Matches are played eight-a-side over two 20-minute halves on smaller pitches, with unlimited substitutions and kick-ins replacing throw-ins. There are no knockout rounds. Instead, after a group stage, teams are placed into one of six performance tiers, with each tier crowning its own winner. Somalia is among 189 FIFA member associations taking part, and one of 78 countries making their first appearance in a FIFA World Cup competition at any level. The tournament runs from October 24 to 30, with most matches staged at the Hovsan Competition Complex and the finals at Baku Crystal Hall. The Somali squad, drawn from a national U-15 championship held earlier this year in Mogadishu and regional states, had been in a centralized training camp for four months under the supervision of the national youth technical staff before departing for Baku. What This Means for Somalia The image of Somali teenagers in Baku, wearing the national jersey and singing a patriotic song after a FIFA victory, is not merely a sports story. It is a counter-narrative to the headlines that usually define Somalia in international media: conflict, famine, piracy, and political dysfunction. For a generation of Somalis who have known little else, the sight of their peers competing on a world stage, and winning, is a powerful affirmation of national identity and potential. The tournament’s development-focused format, with its emphasis on education, life-skills programs, and shared athletes’ villages, is designed to produce exactly this kind of experience. FIFA’s decision to open the competition to nearly all member associations, rather than restricting it to traditional football powers, has given countries like Somalia an opportunity that the senior World Cup has never provided. The victory over Puerto Rico is a single result in a tournament that will ultimately rank teams across six tiers. It will not, by itself, transform Somali football. But it is a beginning, and the players who sang “Somalia belongs to Somalis” in Baku will carry that moment with them, as will the millions of Somalis who watched them. Critical Note The celebration is genuine, and the achievement is real. Somalia’s U-15 team has done something no Somali team has done before: won a match at a FIFA tournament. The players, most aged 13 and 14, have earned the right to sing whatever they want after a victory that their country has waited decades to see. But the moment also invites a question that Somali football must eventually answer. The Somali Football Federation has prioritized youth development, regional leagues, and international exposure. The Baku squad is a product of that policy. The next step, as federation officials have said, is to make this regular rather than exceptional. That will require sustained investment in academies, coaching, and infrastructure, not just a single tournament appearance. For now, the image of Somali teenagers celebrating in Baku is enough. It is a reminder that Somalia’s youth are not defined by the country’s crises. They are defined by what they can achieve when given the chance to compete. The song they sang, “Somalia belongs to Somalis,” is a statement of ownership and belonging. On a football pitch in Azerbaijan, they earned the right to sing it. شارك الزمالك حسام الحارتي تتجه أنظار جماهير الكرة الأفريقية والمصرية نحو سحب قرعة دور المجموعات لبطولة دوري أبطال أفريقيا ، وهي المرحلة التي تمثل البداية الحقيقية للصراع الشرس على عرش الأميرة السمراء. ومع اتضاح معالم التصنيف المبدئي للأندية المتأهلة، يبدو أن ممثلي الكرة المصرية، الزمالك وبيراميدز، يمتلكان أسبقية معنوية وفنية وضعت كلاهما في موقع مريح على رأس التصنيف الأول، مما يفتح أمامهما طريقاً آمناً نسبياً لضمان العبور نحو الأدوار الإقصائية. التصنيف الأول: هيمنة مصرية وتواجد شمال إفريقي قوي استند الاتحاد الإفريقي لكرة القدم (كاف) في تحديد المستويات إلى تراكم النقاط والنتائج التي حققتها الأندية في البطولات القارية خلال السنوات الأخيرة. وجاء التصنيف الأول ليعكس حجم السيطرة المصرية على هذا المستوى: الزمالك.. يتصدر القائمة بفضل تاريخه العريض وتتويجاته القارية الأخيرة. بيراميدز .. يثبت أقدامه كقوة صاعدة واستمرارية في المنافسة القارية. نهضة بركان (المغرب): يتواجد بقوة بفضل نجاحاته الاستثنائية في البطولات الإفريقية. الترجي الرياضي (تونس) الهلال (السودان): منافسة حاسمة على المقعد الرابع ضمن المستوى الأول وفقاً للحسابات الرقمية الأخيرة. يضمن هذا المستوى للزمالك وبيراميدز تجنب المواجهة المباشرة مع عمالقة القارة في هذا الدور، وهو ما يمنح الأجهزة الفنية للفرقاء فرصة لتوزيع المجهود البدني والتركيز على حسم بطاقتي التأهل مبكراً. التصنيف الثاني: أندية الطموح والخبرة الإفريقية يضم التصنيف الثاني أندية متمرسة تمتلك قاعدة جماهيرية عريضة وقدرة عالية على صناعة المفاجآت، مما يجعلها
